endorsements.quote: Institutions should develop emergency plans for major ethical risks and retain the power to suspend or restrict use when model performance declines significantly or specific risks increase.
Complete operational records should be retained so that adverse outcomes are traceable and can inform improvement of models and processes.

They must professionally validate all diagnostic advice, diagnostic conclusions, and treatment plans generated by the model, identify and correct factual deviations and clinical errors, and never substitute AI-generated content for professional judgement.
Final responsibility for medical decisions always rests with healthcare professionals.
Governance should ensure that patients clearly understand AI’s auxiliary role, technical limits, and potential risks.
Patients have rights to information and consent, including the right to know whether and how AI assists decision-making and the right to refuse fully automated decision-making.
Developers and healthcare providers have duties to protect patient rights and promote patient welfare, and these duties should vary according to risk level.
In line with risk-based AI governance, generative medical AI should be subject to graded risk assessment and differentiated access requirements.
Enabling continuous monitoring of medical AI outputs in the real world and real-time identification of risk signals.
At the model development stage, algorithm and model developers carry primary responsibility and should prevent risk at source.
Clinicians should also guard against automation bias, the uncritical acceptance of AI outputs based on perceived technical authority.
Participants must therefore detect new knowledge, perspectives, norms, and concerns and respond in time so that stakeholder concerns can influence decisions [ 58 ].
Developers contribute by designing systems that clearly communicate output uncertainty and technical boundaries to end users.

In public health emergencies in particular, AI-generated medical and health information must undergo both scientific and compliance review to prevent hallucinatory content from causing population-level health misinformation.

Measures include high-quality standards for medical training data to reduce bias, real-time verification against authoritative medical knowledge bases, and integration of medical logic rules into algorithms to suppress hallucination technically.
Before medical AI is used, effective governance mechanisms should be established, tested against adverse situations, and assessed to determine whether they can support necessary interventions [ 44 ].

unlisted_practices: Establish a national technovigilance system, analogous to pharmacovigilance, to monitor hallucination-related adverse events in medical AI.
Give regulators authority to intervene when AI risks exceed thresholds and to require rectification by responsible actors.
Establish adverse-event and hallucination-case reporting systems within healthcare institutions.
Prohibit AI systems from independently diagnosing, automatically issuing prescriptions, or directly making high-risk treatment decisions in clinical use.
Develop regulatory ethical risk assessment guidance for generative AI in healthcare and update it as technology develops.

Coordinate global standards for hallucination definitions, classification, and assessment, and embed hallucination risk warnings and mandatory human-review triggers in exported medical AI technologies.
Involve patients and the public as inputs into AI design and development, and design AI outputs to guide users empathetically toward professional help.

screen.reason: This paper proposes an ethical governance framework (integrating biomedical ethics and Responsible Research and Innovation) to address generative AI hallucinations in healthcare.
